q: Why can a patient with a fracture still walk?
o: A small percentage of fractures are nondisplaced or “hairline” fractures
The absence of pain during walking is the typical presentation
An unrecognized fracture cannot become displaced
All displaced fractures permit painless weight bearing
explanation:
A small percentage of fractures are nondisplaced or “hairline” fractures (p794).

D. All displaced fractures permit painless weight bearing: Most patients cannot bear weight; the ambulatory exception is a small nondisplaced subset (p794).
C. An unrecognized fracture cannot become displaced: An unrecognized nondisplaced fracture may progress to displacement (p794).
B. The absence of pain during walking is the typical presentation: The ambulatory subset can walk with pain, not necessarily without pain (p794).

q: What imaging follows negative radiographs when fracture remains suspected?
o: Plain radiographs alone exclude a fracture
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
No further imaging after negative plain radiographs
Computed tomography
explanation:
MRI should follow negative plain radiographs when fracture remains suspected because it detects marrow edema and fracture more sensitively than CT (p794).

D. Computed tomography: MRI is more sensitive than CT in this setting (p794).
C. No further imaging after negative plain radiographs: The book specifically calls for MRI when radiographs are negative (p794).
A. Plain radiographs alone exclude a fracture: Negative radiographs do not end evaluation; MRI looks for marrow edema and fracture (p794).

q: Why is arthroplasty commonly used for displaced femoral-neck fractures?
o: Femoral-neck vascular disruption can cause nonunion and osteonecrosis
Displaced femoral-neck fractures cannot disrupt the retinacular arteries
The femoral neck has the plentiful and redundant blood supply described for intertrochanteric fractures
Internal fixation eliminates the risk of femoral-head osteonecrosis
explanation:
Femoral-neck fractures can disrupt the blood supply, causing nonunion and osteonecrosis; displaced fractures are therefore usually managed with arthroplasty (p794).

C. The femoral neck has the plentiful and redundant blood supply described for intertrochanteric fractures: This transfers the intertrochanteric vascular advantage to the femoral neck (p794).
B. Displaced femoral-neck fractures cannot disrupt the retinacular arteries: The delicate vessels lie closely against the neck and can be disrupted (p794).
D. Internal fixation eliminates the risk of femoral-head osteonecrosis: The vascular risk is why displaced neck fractures are usually treated with arthroplasty (p794).

q: Why does internal fixation suit intertrochanteric fractures?
o: Its blood supply depends on the delicate vessels closely apposed to the femoral neck
Internal fixation requires replacing the joint with an arthroplasty
Nonunion and osteonecrosis are more common in this region
The blood supply to the intertrochanteric area is plentiful and redundant
explanation:
The intertrochanteric blood supply is plentiful and redundant, allowing fractures to heal well after internal fixation (p794).

A. Its blood supply depends on the delicate vessels closely apposed to the femoral neck: That is the femoral-neck/head vascular pattern, contrasted with the intertrochanteric area (p794).
C. Nonunion and osteonecrosis are more common in this region: They are less common in the intertrochanteric region (p794).
B. Internal fixation requires replacing the joint with an arthroplasty: The book distinguishes fixation with a plate/screw or intramedullary screw from joint replacement (p794).

q: What does the chapter report about mortality with general versus spinal anesthesia?
o: Spinal anesthesia has lower mortality than general anesthesia
No differences have been found in mortality between general and spinal anesthetic.
General anesthesia has lower mortality than spinal anesthesia
Both are excluded because hip fractures are normally managed without surgery
explanation:
The chapter reports no mortality difference between general and spinal anesthesia for hip-fracture surgery (p797).

C. General anesthesia has lower mortality than spinal anesthesia: The book reports no mortality difference (p797).
A. Spinal anesthesia has lower mortality than general anesthesia: The book reports no mortality difference (p797).
D. Both are excluded because hip fractures are normally managed without surgery: The majority undergo surgical repair, and no mortality difference between these anesthetics was found (p797).

q: What balance should postoperative analgesia achieve?
o: Routine intravenous medication because preoperative nerve blocks cannot help after surgery
Relief only at rest, without anticipating therapy-related pain
Sustained early pain relief, minimal sedation, and anticipation of therapy-related pain
Maximal sedation regardless of participation in therapy
explanation:
Postoperative analgesia should provide sustained early pain relief, minimize sedation, and anticipate episodic pain during activities such as therapy (p797).

D. Maximal sedation regardless of participation in therapy: The regimen should minimize sedation and support mobility/therapy (p797).
B. Relief only at rest, without anticipating therapy-related pain: The regimen should anticipate episodic increases during activities (p797).
A. Routine intravenous medication because preoperative nerve blocks cannot help after surgery: Preoperative nerve blocks often help postoperative pain and IV medication is not required after surgery (p797).

q: What should precede a bisphosphonate when vitamin D is deficient?
o: Replete vitamin D before starting the bisphosphonate
Avoid checking vitamin D during the acute admission
Leave vitamin D deficiency untreated if rehabilitation is planned
Start the bisphosphonate before correcting vitamin D deficiency
explanation:
Vitamin D should be repleted before starting a bisphosphonate when treating osteoporosis after hip fracture (p798).

D. Start the bisphosphonate before correcting vitamin D deficiency: The stated order is vitamin D repletion first (p798).
C. Leave vitamin D deficiency untreated if rehabilitation is planned: Repletion is specified before the bisphosphonate; rehabilitation does not replace it (p798).
B. Avoid checking vitamin D during the acute admission: The level should be checked during admission if not measured recently (p798).

q: How long does this chapter recommend continuing postoperative DVT prophylaxis?
o: 24 to 48 hours
21 to 31 days
At least 6 months
1 to 5 days
explanation:
The chapter recommends continuing DVT prophylaxis for 21 to 31 days after hip-fracture surgery (p801).

D. 1 to 5 days: This is the usual acute postoperative hospital stay (p797); the requested value is 21 to 31 days (p801).
C. At least 6 months: This is the exercise-program duration for peripheral arterial disease benefit (p830); the requested value is 21 to 31 days (p801).
A. 24 to 48 hours: This is the earliest stroke-rehabilitation interval once stable (p831); the requested value is 21 to 31 days (p801).
